question: Your customer support agent is scored on a labeled evaluation set of 700 return requests, 250 account issues, and 50 billing disputes. A conversation passes when the agent chooses the correct outcome. After a system prompt change, the overall pass rate rises from 92% to 95%. The team reports only this overall figure. Which conclusion does this result support?

options.text: It shows nothing useful, because accuracy on a labeled evaluation set says nothing about how the agent will handle live customer requests in production.
options.reason: The guide relies on labeled validation sets to measure accuracy; the limit of this result is that it is aggregated, not that it comes from labeled data.

options.text: It supports a gain for the set as a whole, but it cannot show that billing disputes held steady, because 50 cases barely move the overall figure.
options.reason: An aggregate score can mask poor performance on a small segment, so a decline on the 50 billing disputes could sit inside the higher overall pass rate.

options.text: It shows that the new prompt is at least as accurate for every request type, because a gain on one fixed evaluation set cannot hide a drop in any single type.
options.reason: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on a specific segment, and billing disputes are only 5% of the set, so a drop there would barely move the overall figure.

options.text: It shows that billing disputes improved the most, because the gain is likely to come from the request type that is hardest to resolve and has the most room to grow.
options.reason: An overall figure does not reveal which segment changed, so the result gives no evidence about billing disputes; only a per-type breakdown could show that.
